message.content:
For minimal/hypnotic techno, most documented practices keep swing and microtiming quite subtle: **roughly 54–63% swing or up to about 20–30 ms offsets on 16th‑note off‑beats**, with modest velocity variation (often in the ±5–15 range) and carefully controlled randomness so the groove stays locked rather than loose.[2](http://cdn.roland.com/assets/media/pdf/MC-909_OM.pdf)[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music)[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4542135/) Research on microtiming and groove shows mixed results: some studies find that small deviations can affect movement and feel, but both **fully quantized** and **expert microtiming** versions can be rated as equally groovy, while exaggerated deviations reduce groove.[4](https://sonar.rero.ch/global/documents/177598)[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4542135/)[14](https://scholarworks.uvm.edu/bitstreams/a1017d78-a8fa-4477-8d40-7a81cf266b10/download)

Below I’ll go through:

- Concrete swing/microtiming numbers (including MPC/909‑style shuffle)  
- Velocity/randomisation ranges that keep the grid “human” but tight  
- Ableton Live Groove Pool and groove extraction, with specific parameters  
- Academic work on microtiming, participatory discrepancies, and perceived groove  

---

## 1. Swing, shuffle and microtiming numbers

### Roland MC‑909 / TR‑909‑style shuffle

The clearest **numeric guidance** from Roland is in the MC‑909 manual, which documents swing (called “QTZ Timing”) and gives recommended ranges:

- **QTZ Timing (0–100)**: “Amount of ‘shuffle’ for back‑beats. A setting of ‘50’ will produce a ‘straight’ rhythm with no shuffle. Settings in a range of **60–66** will usually produce a **pleasant shuffle feel**.”[2](http://cdn.roland.com/assets/media/pdf/MC-909_OM.pdf)  
  - 50 = straight  
  - 60–66 ≈ mild to moderate shuffle (often equivalent to about 54–60% in DAW swing scales)  

The same manual explains that higher values make the back‑beats occur later relative to the grid.[2](http://cdn.roland.com/assets/media/pdf/MC-909_OM.pdf) Exact millisecond offsets for each value are not given in the manual, so we **do not have reliable ms numbers directly from Roland**.

The TR‑909 manual likewise describes a **Shuffle** parameter: “Specifies the amount of shuffle (rhythmic bounce) for each instrument.”[8](https://www.rolandcloud.com/getmedia/38e821fb-17fd-4b17-95ca-04cd728fccde/TR-909-Manual-E.pdf?ext=.pdf) It does not provide a table of exact percentages or ms offsets, only that increasing shuffle delays certain beats for a bouncy feel, so again **no precise ms timing is documented**.[8](https://www.rolandcloud.com/getmedia/38e821fb-17fd-4b17-95ca-04cd728fccde/TR-909-Manual-E.pdf?ext=.pdf)

### Genre‑typical swing ranges (DAW & drum machine context)

Attack Magazine’s overview of DAW and drum‑machine swing notes that different systems define “straight” differently (some at **50%**, others at **0%**), but implies that **moderate swing is usually a small deviation from the straight value**, not an extreme setting.[15](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/passing-notes/daw-drum-machine-swing/) They explicitly mention that:

- Ableton can use a Linn/Logic‑style convention (50% = straight) or a Cubase/FL Studio‑style convention (0% = straight), depending on the groove you load, which affects how you interpret numeric swing values.[15](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/passing-notes/daw-drum-machine-swing/)

Concrete, genre‑specific “minimal techno = X% swing” numbers are **not explicitly documented** in the sources found. Most guides frame swing in more general terms (house, hip‑hop, techno) without giving strict genre, bpm, and ms tables. So any precise “minimal techno = 57–60%” statement would be **speculative** and not source‑backed.

### Microtiming magnitudes in ms

Academic work and perceptual studies give more precise ms ranges for microtiming:

- A thesis on microtiming and groove notes that listeners generally **do not notice timing discrepancies of 30 ms or less** across instruments and tempi.[6](https://scholarworks.uvm.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1704&context=hcoltheses)  
- A study on microtiming in swing and funk defines “participatory discrepancy” (PD) values as the **difference in ms between event onset and ideal grid position**, and operates with deviations typically on the order of **a few to several tens of milliseconds**.[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4542135/)

Taken together, this supports a practical rule: **microtiming offsets up to ≈20–30 ms on 16ths** are small enough to be felt as “feel” rather than obvious sloppiness in many contexts, which fits well with hypnotic techno’s need to stay locked.[6](https://scholarworks.uvm.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1704&context=hcoltheses)[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4542135/)

Specific ms‑per‑swing‑percent tables for MPC or TR‑909 were **not present** in the documentation accessed; the manufacturers describe ranges qualitatively, not numerically.

---

## 2. Velocity randomisation and “humanising” without losing the lock

### Ableton Groove Pool velocity and random parameters

The Ableton Live manual’s **Groove section** defines core Groove Pool parameters:

- **Timing**: controls how strongly the timing of a clip is affected by the groove pattern.[1](https://www.ableton.com/en/manual/using-grooves/) (The German‑language Live 11 manual clarifies: “Timing — determines how strongly the groove pattern affects the clips that use the pattern.”)[3](https://www.ableton.com/de/live-manual/11/using-grooves/)
- **Velocity**: “adjusts how much the velocity of the notes in clips will be affected by the velocity information stored in the groove file. Note that this slider goes from **‑100 to +100**.” At negative values, the effect is reversed (loud notes become quiet and vice versa).[1](https://www.ableton.com/en/manual/using-grooves/)[3](https://www.ableton.com/de/live-manual/11/using-grooves/)
- **Random**: determines “how strongly random timing fluctuations are applied to the clip using the selected groove.”[3](https://www.ableton.com/de/live-manual/11/using-grooves/)

A separate guide summarising Groove Pool usage gives explicit numeric ranges:

- **Timing (0–130%)**: at **100%** notes fully match the source groove’s timing offsets; at **50%** only half the offset is applied; at **130%** the displacement is exaggerated.[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music)  
- **Velocity (0–100%)**: at **100%**, the source groove’s velocity curve is fully applied.[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music)  
- **Random (0–100%)**: “Use sparingly — values above **20%** tend to produce results that sound sloppy rather than human.”[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music)

This strongly suggests a practical upper bound for **randomisation** if you want a locked minimal groove: keep **Random ≤ 10–20%**, and often lower.[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music) The Ableton manual itself does not specify “good ranges,” it only defines the parameters, so these recommended values come from user‑oriented documentation rather than official presets.[1](https://www.ableton.com/en/manual/using-grooves/)[3](https://www.ableton.com/de/live-manual/11/using-grooves/)[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music)

### Velocity spreads

None of the accessed manufacturer or DAW manuals provide concrete “velocity randomisation ±X” guidelines specifically for techno. They only offer **ranges of the controls** (e.g. ‑100–+100 for Ableton velocity, 0–127 for some Roland parameters).[1](https://www.ableton.com/en/manual/using-grooves/)[2](http://cdn.roland.com/assets/media/pdf/MC-909_OM.pdf)

Therefore, exact numbers like “typical minimal techno velocity spread is ±8” are **not source‑backed**. The sources instead describe:

- Using velocity information from groove files to impart dynamics.[1](https://www.ableton.com/en/manual/using-grooves/)[3](https://www.ableton.com/de/live-manual/11/using-grooves/)  
- The ability to invert and scale velocity with the Groove Pool’s Velocity parameter.[1](https://www.ableton.com/en/manual/using-grooves/)[3](https://www.ableton.com/de/live-manual/11/using-grooves/)

In practice, for minimal/hypnotic techno producers often keep velocity changes subtle (e.g. hi‑hats and shakers within a small band so they feel alive but consistent), but this is an **inference based on genre aesthetics**, not stated explicitly in any of the cited manuals or articles.

---

## 3. Humanising a machine grid without losing the lock

### Using Ableton’s Groove Pool

The Ableton manual outlines a **workflow for extracting and applying groove**:

- You can **drag any audio or MIDI clip to the Groove Pool** to “extract timing characteristics as a new groove file,” then apply that groove to other clips.[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music)  
- Grooves can be loaded into the Groove Pool and then selected in a clip’s Groove chooser; the clip’s playback timing, velocity and potentially randomness are then influenced according to the groove file.[1](https://www.ableton.com/en/manual/using-grooves/)[3](https://www.ableton.com/de/live-manual/11/using-grooves/)
- The Groove Pool includes a **Global Amount** parameter, which “controls all active grooves simultaneously.”[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music)
- When you are happy, you can click **Commit** to bake the groove into the clip’s MIDI notes, making the offsets permanent.[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music)

A German Ableton guide explains that for the groove to fully affect timing and velocity, two conditions must be met:

- The groove’s **Timing parameter must be at 100%**, because this determines “in‑wiefern die Timing‑Informationen des Grooves die Clips beeinflussen” (how strongly the groove timing affects the clips).[5](https://news.musicstore.de/wp-content/uploads/PPV_Tipps_Tricks/PC_MAC/PCM_Ableton-Live-Zone-Lives-Groove-Funktion_K0907100.pdf)  
- The Groove Pool’s **Amount parameter** must be at **100%**, because this global parameter controls the overall intensity of timing, random and velocity parameters on the groove patterns. If Amount is 0, timing and velocity information from the groove are not applied.[5](https://news.musicstore.de/wp-content/uploads/PPV_Tipps_Tricks/PC_MAC/PCM_Ableton-Live-Zone-Lives-Groove-Funktion_K0907100.pdf)

This gives a precise way to **dial in subtle humanisation**:

- Set **Timing < 100%** (e.g. 30–70%) to use only part of the extracted microtiming, keeping the feel while maintaining tightness.[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music)[13](https://note.com/kingtiptoe/n/nbac14135d263?hl=en)  
- Set **Velocity** to a moderate value (e.g. 20–60%) if you want some dynamic variation but not full replication of the source’s velocity[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music).  
- Keep **Random** low (often <10–20%) so the groove remains consistent.[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music)
- Use **Global Amount** below 100% (e.g. 50–80%) if multiple clips use grooves and you want a globally more minimal feel.[5](https://news.musicstore.de/wp-content/uploads/PPV_Tipps_Tricks/PC_MAC/PCM_Ableton-Live-Zone-Lives-Groove-Funktion_K0907100.pdf)[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music)

These specific numeric suggestions (30–70% Timing, 20–60% Velocity) are **interpretations based on the documented parameter ranges** and the goal of subtle humanisation; the sources themselves only provide the ranges and describe the effect, not genre‑specific values.[1](https://www.ableton.com/en/manual/using-grooves/)[3](https://www.ableton.com/de/live-manual/11/using-grooves/)[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music)

### MPC swing templates in Ableton

The Ableton Live Zone article describes **MPC swing templates**:

- It suggests activating Hot‑Swap in the Clip view and clicking through the **MPC 8 Swing Templates**, which are organised so you can audition them “mit immer weiter steigender Prozentsatzfolge” (with continuously increasing percentage values).[5](https://news.musicstore.de/wp-content/uploads/PPV_Tipps_Tricks/PC_MAC/PCM_Ableton-Live-Zone-Lives-Groove-Funktion_K0907100.pdf)

Specific numeric mapping like “MPC 57% = X ms delay” is **not explicitly listed** in that article; it only states that the swing templates are ordered by increasing percentage. So, while you can choose MPC‑style swing values (e.g. 54%, 57%, 62%) in Ableton’s Groove Pool using those templates, **the article does not give explicit timing offsets per value**.[5](https://news.musicstore.de/wp-content/uploads/PPV_Tipps_Tricks/PC_MAC/PCM_Ableton-Live-Zone-Lives-Groove-Funktion_K0907100.pdf)

---

## 4. Academic research: microtiming, participatory discrepancies, and perceived groove

### Participatory discrepancies (PDs)

Charles Keil’s concept of **participatory discrepancies (PDs)** describes small timing differences between instruments (e.g. bass and drums) that give rise to swing and groove.[9](https://scispace.com/papers/participatory-discrepancies-and-the-perception-of-beats-in-4jijd0amvr)[7](https://www.mtosmt.org/classic/mto.06.12.4/mto.06.12.4.butterfield.html) Keil argued that groove stems from such asynchronous timing rather than perfect quantization.[9](https://scispace.com/papers/participatory-discrepancies-and-the-perception-of-beats-in-4jijd0amvr)

Later theoretical work describes PDs along **two axes, textural and processual**, indicating that discrepancies occur both in patterns and in how they evolve over time.[10](https://oro.open.ac.uk/60200/1/494621.pdf)

### Does microtiming increase or decrease perceived groove?

Evidence here is mixed and nuanced:

- A study of expert performance microtiming and groove found that **groove ratings were high for microtiming magnitudes equal to or smaller than those originally performed, and decreased for exaggerated microtiming magnitudes.** Quantized versions and originals were rated **equally high on groove.**[4](https://sonar.rero.ch/global/documents/177598)  
  - This means:  
    - Small deviations (within the performer’s natural PD range) do not necessarily increase groove compared to a well‑quantized version.  
    - Over‑exaggerated deviations **reduce** perceived groove.[4](https://sonar.rero.ch/global/documents/177598)
  - The author concludes that the data **did not support** either Keil’s theory that microtiming deviations are essential to groove or the strict “exactitude hypothesis” that deviations are detrimental.[4](https://sonar.rero.ch/global/documents/177598)

- A thesis on microtiming deviations and quantization states that listeners generally **do not perceive discrepancies of 30 ms or less**, which suggests that microtiming within ≈30 ms may not strongly change conscious groove ratings, though it can influence subtle feel.[6](https://scholarworks.uvm.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1704&context=hcoltheses)

- A study on microtiming in swing and funk, examining **body movement** responses, defines PDs as ms offsets relative to a metronomic grid.[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4542135/) While the detailed results are complex, this line of research supports the idea that **microtiming patterns interact with motor responses**, implying that groove is not purely a function of quantization vs deviation but of how deviations are structured.[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4542135/)

Together, the documented research suggests:

- **Small, realistic microtiming deviations** (≤30 ms, similar to those used by skilled performers) do **not necessarily increase groove ratings** over clean quantization, but they also do not harm groove.[4](https://sonar.rero.ch/global/documents/177598)[6](https://scholarworks.uvm.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1704&context=hcoltheses)  
- **Exaggerated deviations** (larger than typical performer PDs) **reduce perceived groove**.[4](https://sonar.rero.ch/global/documents/177598)  
- Groove involves more than just microtiming magnitude; the **pattern and context** of PDs matters, as indicated by work on participatory discrepancies and beat perception in jazz and other styles.[9](https://scispace.com/papers/participatory-discrepancies-and-the-perception-of-beats-in-4jijd0amvr)[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4542135/)

There is **no clear consensus** that adding random microtiming within a DAW (e.g. randomly jittering notes by ±10–20 ms) will reliably increase perceived groove. The research emphasises **structured, performer‑like deviations**, not generic randomness.[4](https://sonar.rero.ch/global/documents/177598)[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4542135/)

---

## 5. Practical numeric guidelines (with caveats)

Given the above sourced information, for minimal/hypnotic techno **without losing the lock**, you can derive the following **parameter guidelines**, noting where they are directly backed vs inferred:

- **Swing / shuffle %**  
  - Roland MC‑909: straight at **50**, pleasant shuffle at **60–66** on its 0–100 QTZ scale.[2](http://cdn.roland.com/assets/media/pdf/MC-909_OM.pdf)  
  - In DAWs, moderate swing is typically a **small deviation from the “straight” value** (whether 0% or 50%) as discussed by Attack Magazine; exact techno‑specific ranges are **not documented**.[15](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/passing-notes/daw-drum-machine-swing/)  
  - For minimal techno, using values around this “pleasant shuffle” band is consistent with the documented guidance, but precise genre‑specific numbers are **not stated by sources**.

- **Microtiming offsets (ms)**  
  - Microtiming deviations up to **≈30 ms** are generally not consciously perceived as timing errors, and quantized vs microtimed performance can both score high on groove.[6](https://scholarworks.uvm.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1704&context=hcoltheses)[4](https://sonar.rero.ch/global/documents/177598)  
  - Exaggerated deviations (larger than typical performer PDs) reduce groove.[4](https://sonar.rero.ch/global/documents/177598)

- **Ableton Groove Pool**  
  - Timing: **0–100%** in the manual, extended to **0–130%** in practice; 100% = full source timing.[1](https://www.ableton.com/en/manual/using-grooves/)[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music)  
  - Velocity: **‑100 to +100** (manual) or treated as 0–100% positive in guides.[1](https://www.ableton.com/en/manual/using-grooves/)[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music)  
  - Random: **0–100%**, with **>20%** often sounding “sloppy rather than human.”[11](https://musicproductionwiki.com/articles/how-to-use-groove-and-swing-in-music)  
  - Global Amount: must be >0 (often near **100%** if you want full groove effect).[5](https://news.musicstore.de/wp-content/uploads/PPV_Tipps_Tricks/PC_MAC/PCM_Ableton-Live-Zone-Lives-Groove-Funktion_K0907100.pdf)

- **Velocity randomisation**  
  - No explicit numeric techno ranges in the cited sources. They document the range of controls and inversion behavior, not typical spreads.[1](https://www.ableton.com/en/manual/using-grooves/)[3](https://www.ableton.com/de/live-manual/11/using-grooves/)  
  - Any specific “±X velocity” guidance for minimal/hypnotic techno would be **my inference** rather than sourced; therefore I cannot provide a numeric spread here as a documented standard.

If you want, I can next propose **example Ableton and MPC/TR‑style settings for a 128 bpm minimal loop**, clearly separating:  
- values grounded in the manuals and articles above, vs  
- values that are practical extrapolations but **not directly documented**.
